paragraphs: The doctor stepped out of the room again, wrapped in his fur coat, his cap already on. He looked almost angry and disgusted, as if he feared catching some dirt. He threw a quick look around the passage and eyed Alyosha and Kolya sternly. Alyosha waved to the coachman from the doorway, and the carriage that had brought the doctor rolled up. The captain rushed out behind the doctor and, bowing and apologizing, caught him for one last word. The poor man looked totally crushed. His eyes were frightened.

“Your Excellency, your Excellency ... is it possible?” he began, but he couldn’t go on and wrung his hands in despair. Still he kept his eyes fixed on the doctor, pleading, as if a single word from him could yet change the poor boy’s fate.
“I can’t help it. I’m not God!” the doctor answered casually, though in his usual pompous manner.
“Doctor ... your Excellency ... will it be soon? Soon?”
“You must be ready for anything,” said the doctor, stressing each word and cutting it off short. He dropped his eyes and was about to step out to the carriage.
“Your Excellency, for Christ’s sake!” the captain, panic-stricken, held him back once more. “Your Excellency! Is there really nothing, nothing at all, that can save him now?”

“It’s no longer in my hands,” said the doctor impatiently, “but, h’m!...” He broke off suddenly. “If you could, say ... send ... your patient ... right away, without delay” (and the words “right away, without delay” came out with such angry sternness that the captain flinched) “to Syracuse, the change to the new, be-ne-ficial climate might perhaps bring about—”
“To Syracuse!” cried the captain, who could not make sense of it.
“Syracuse is in Sicily,” Kolya blurted out, by way of explanation. The doctor turned to look at him.
“Sicily! Your Excellency,” the captain stammered, “but you’ve seen”—he spread out his hands at his surroundings—“mamma and my family?”

“N—no, Sicily is no place for the family. The family ought to go to the Caucasus in early spring ... your daughter must go to the Caucasus, and your wife ... once she has taken the waters there for her rheumatism ... has to be sent straight on to Paris, to the mental specialist Lepelletier. I can give you a note for him, and then ... there may be a change—”
“Doctor, doctor! But look!” Again the captain threw out his hands in despair, pointing at the bare wooden walls of the passage.
“Well, that’s no concern of mine,” the doctor grinned. “You asked what treatment was possible, and I’ve told you what medical science says. As for the rest, I’m sorry to say—”

“Don’t be afraid, apothecary, my dog won’t bite you,” Kolya snapped loudly. He had noticed the doctor’s nervous glance at Perezvon, who stood in the doorway. Kolya’s voice was full of anger. He used the word apothecary instead of doctor on purpose and later explained that he used it “to insult him.”
“What was that?” The doctor jerked his head up and stared at Kolya in astonishment. “Who is this?” he asked Alyosha, as if demanding an explanation.
“I’m Perezvon’s master. Don’t mind me,” Kolya said sharply again.
“Perezvon?”[7] the doctor repeated, bewildered.
“He hears the bell, but where it is he cannot tell. Good-by, we’ll meet in Syracuse.”
“Who is this? Who is this?” The doctor went into a towering rage.

“He’s a schoolboy, doctor, a naughty boy. Pay no attention to him,” said Alyosha, frowning and talking fast. “Kolya, be quiet!” he cried to Krassotkin. “Pay no attention to him, doctor,” he said again, with some impatience.
“He wants a whipping, a good whipping!” The doctor stamped his foot, in a perfect fury.
“And you know, apothecary, Perezvon might bite!” said Kolya, pale now, his voice shaking and his eyes blazing. “_Ici_, Perezvon!”
“Kolya, one more word and I’m finished with you,” Alyosha cried in a tone that allowed no argument.
“Only one man in the world can give orders to Nikolay Krassotkin, and here he is”; Kolya pointed at Alyosha. “I obey him. Good-by!”

He strode forward, opened the door and went straight into the inner room, with Perezvon flying after him. The doctor stood rooted to the spot for five seconds, staring at Alyosha in amazement. Then, with a curse, he hurried out to the carriage, saying aloud over and over, “This is ... this is ... I don’t know what this is!” The captain rushed ahead to help him into the carriage. Alyosha went after Kolya into the room. Kolya was already beside Ilusha’s bed. The sick boy was holding his hand and calling for his father. A minute later the captain came back in too.

“Father, father, come ... we ...” Ilusha stammered in great agitation. He seemed unable to go on, so he threw his thin arms around his father and Kolya, pulled them together into one embrace and held them as hard as he could. The captain suddenly began to shake with silent sobs, and Kolya’s lips and chin trembled.
“Father, father! I feel so sorry for you!” Ilusha moaned bitterly.
“Ilusha ... darling ... the doctor said ... you’ll be all right ... we’ll be happy ... the doctor ...” the captain began.
“Ah, father! I know what the new doctor told you about me.... I saw it!” cried Ilusha, and once more he hugged them both with all his strength and hid his face against his father’s shoulder.
“Father, don’t cry. And when I die, find yourself a good boy, another one ... pick one out of all of them, a good one, call him Ilusha, and love him in my place....”
“Quiet, old man, you’ll get well,” Krassotkin burst out, in a voice that sounded cross.

“But don’t ever forget me, father,” Ilusha went on. “Come to my grave ... and, father, bury me by our big stone, where we used to walk, and come to me there in the evening, you and Krassotkin ... and Perezvon ... I’ll be waiting for you.... Father, father!”
His voice gave out. The three of them said nothing, still holding each other. Nina was crying softly in her chair, and finally, when she saw them all in tears, “mamma” started to weep too.
“Ilusha! Ilusha!” she cried.
Krassotkin suddenly freed himself from Ilusha’s arms.

“Good-by, old man, mother expects me home for dinner,” he said in a rush. “What a shame I didn’t tell her! She’ll be terribly worried.... But after dinner I’ll come straight back to you for the whole day, the whole evening, and I’ll tell you all sorts of things, all sorts of things. And I’ll bring Perezvon. I’ll take him with me now, though, because he’d start howling once I’m gone and would only trouble you. Good-by!”
He ran out into the passage. He hadn’t wanted to cry, but out there he burst into tears. Alyosha found him weeping.
“Kolya, you must be sure to keep your word and come back, or he’ll be terribly disappointed,” Alyosha told him firmly.
“I will! Oh, how I curse myself for not coming sooner!” Kolya muttered through his tears, not even ashamed of them any more.
Just then the captain flew out of the room and pulled the door shut behind him. He looked frantic, and his lips were shaking. He stood before the two of them and threw up his arms.

“I don’t want a good boy! I don’t want another boy!” he muttered in a wild whisper, grinding his teeth. “If I forget thee, Jerusalem, may my tongue—” His voice broke in a sob, and he dropped to his knees before the wooden bench. He pressed his fists to his head and began to sob with absurd, whimpering cries, struggling to keep them from being heard in the room.
Kolya ran out into the street.
“Good-by, Karamazov? Are you coming yourself?” he called out sharply and angrily to Alyosha.
“Yes, I’ll come this evening, for certain.”
“What was it he said about Jerusalem?... What did he mean?”
“It’s from the Bible. ‘If I forget thee, Jerusalem’ means, if I forget what is dearest to me, if I let anything take its place, then may—”
“I see, that’s enough! Be sure you come! _Ici_, Perezvon!” he shouted at the dog with real ferocity, and with long quick strides he set off for home.
